cues.text: The Fall of the Templars
In October 1307, King Philip IV of France , deeply in debt to the Order of the Knights Templar and covetous of its considerable wealth, ordered their sudden mass arrest throughout France.
The Templars faced charges of heresy, idolatry, and immorality.
Confessions extracted under torture were later retracted by the order's own members.

Pope Clement V , the first pope to reside at Avignon and heavily dependent on French royal favor, faced enormous pressure to endorse Philip's actions against an order answering, in principle, directly to the papacy rather than any king.
To settle the Templars' fate and address other pressing business, Clement summoned a general council to meet at Vienne , in southeastern France, by the bull Regnans in coelis of August 1308.
A Council Under Royal Pressure
The council opened on October 16, 1311 with some twenty cardinals, four patriarchs, roughly a hundred archbishops and bishops, and numerous abbots and priors in attendance.

A commission investigating the charges against the Templars found the evidence against the order as a whole unconvincing, and the majority of council fathers favored allowing the Templars a formal defense rather than immediate suppression.
King Philip, unwilling to accept any outcome short of the order's abolition, appeared at Vienne in person in February 1312 with a great armed retinue and pressed the pope directly for suppression.
Faced with this show of royal force, Clement abandoned the judicial process and resolved instead to dissolve the order by papal administrative act rather than by a formal finding of guilt.
Suppression Without Conviction
On March 22, 1312 , Clement announced his decision to the assembled cardinals.
The bull of suppression, Vox in excelso , dissolved the Order of the Temple not on the basis of proven heresy.
As the text carefully stated, it acted out of provision and pastoral solicitude for the good of the Church.

At the council's second formal session on April 3, with Philip and his sons present, the suppression was formally promulgated; further bulls in May transferred most of the order's property to the rival Knights Hospitaller.
The council also took up the long-simmering matter of Pope Boniface VIII , formally declaring him to have been a lawful pope.

It absolved him of the charges of heresy that Philip's agents had leveled against his memory years earlier, while separately absolving Philip himself of responsibility for his actions against Boniface.
Other Business
Beyond the Templar affair, the council addressed the condition of the Holy Land and discussed a new crusade that never materialized.
It also examined the teachings of the Beguines and Beghards , lay religious movements whose more radical adherents were suspected of doctrinal errors related to the heresy known as the Free Spirit.
Several of the council's decrees, later collected as the Clementine Constitutions , also addressed university education and clerical discipline.
The council closed on May 6, 1312 , having accomplished the political objective Philip IV had demanded, if not through the judicial process the assembled bishops had initially favored.
Legacy
The Council of Vienne is remembered above all for the suppression of the Templars.

Historians have long regarded this episode as a stark illustration of how far a medieval king's political and financial interests could override the ordinary workings of ecclesiastical justice, even at a general council of the universal Church.

Clement V's careful choice to dissolve rather than condemn the order — avoiding a formal ruling on their guilt — has itself become a matter of historical debate about the true weight of the evidence against the Templars.

The council's other work, though less remembered, contributed lasting canonical legislation through the Clementine Constitutions, incorporated into the Church's body of canon law for centuries afterward.
